newsitem.title: USA: Buddhist sect behind money for Clinton defense.
newsitem.headline: Buddhist sect behind money for Clinton defense.

text.p: A Buddhist sect, led by a Vietnamese woman who now lives in Taiwan, was the source of almost $800,000 in contributions to President Bill Clinton's legal defence fund, a Senate committee heard on Thursday.
The Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, investigating foreign fund raising in the 1996 elections, heard testimony about the sect from two private investigators and a member of the group.

The investigators, Terry Lenzner and Lauren Berger of Investigative Group Inc. were hired by the Presidential Legal Expense Trust to look into the source of funds delivered last year by Yah Lin "Charlie" Trie, a former Little Rock, Arkansas, restaurant owner who was friendly with Clinton.

Berger said she quickly established that the source of the money for the Legal Expenses Trust were members of the Suma Ching Hai, a Buddhist group with 100,000 adherents throughout the world, including several thousand Americans.

In a report prepared for the Trust and entered into the committee record, Berger described the group's beliefs and methods of meditation. She quoted from the accounts of two U.S. experts who described the group as a "cult" which put pressure on its members to donate money.
The group's leader, Ching Hai, describes herself as a "living Buddha" and encourages her followers to chant her name during meditation.

The group's New York contact person, Zhi Hua Dong, later told the committee the organisation consisted of "the Enlightened Master Suma Ching Hai and a group of devoted followers, just like 2,000 years ago Jesus with a bunch of followers."

Dong described how he was contacted last year by one of Ching Hai's attendants and asked to buy money orders for a meeting the following day, March 16, 1996. He and a small group of friends bought about $70,000 in money orders.

The next day, Ching Hai arrived with Trie, who was initiated into the sect that evening. She told American members of the group that Clinton was a good person "who needed about $2 million for his legal expenses. She could not help him personally because she was not an American citizen but they could help," Dong testified.

Later that evening, Dong testified, he met Ching Hai and Trie in her hotel room and they spread out the takings, together with the proceeds of other fund raising events she had held for the Clinton legal defence fund.
Dong said there was possibly $400,000 spread on the table in checks and money orders.

Trie first appeared in the Legal Expenses Trust's office in March 1996 and dumped $460,000 in personal checks and money orders for $1,000 apiece or less on the table. He later tried to donate two additional instalments totalling $329,000.

Clinton and his wife have run up millions of dollars in personal legal fees relating to the Whitewater land affair and a sexual harrassment suit filed against Clinton by former Arkansas state employee Paula Corbin Jones.
The Clinton Legal Expenses Trust ultimately rejected all the donations collected by Trie, but has been criticised for keeping this secret until after the 1996 election.
At about the time he was trying to give money for Clinton's legal bills, Trie simultaneously contributed $220,000 to the Democratic Party.
That money came illegally from a business associate in the Portuguese colony of Macau. Trie is currently in China and has refused to return to the United States or answer questions.
